title: He thought the King forgot him.
paragraphs: He thought the King forgot him.
But the King was already calling his name.
Somewhere in Lo-debar… hidden, limping, surviving on silence… a man carried a story soaked in shame.
And if we’re honest—
So do we.
Because not all brokenness is visible.

Some of us walk fine… but inside, we’re collapsing.
Smiling in public… but negotiating with compromise in private.
Serving in ministry… but secretly tired, numb, drifting.
And we call that “normal.”
But heaven calls it hiding.
Mephibosheth wasn’t just physically crippled—his identity was buried under loss. Son of Jonathan. Grandson of Saul. Royal blood… reduced to survival mode.
Because when his world fell apart, someone dropped him.

Five years old.
Carried… then broken.
Chosen… then forgotten.
And now he lives in Lo-debar—a place scholars often describe as “no pasture,” “no word,” “no provision.”
A dry place.
A silent place.
A place where purpose feels like a memory.
Let me ask you something—
Have you built a life in Lo-debar and called it peace?
Have you learned to function in dryness so long that you stopped expecting God to move?
Here’s the part that will wreck you:
Grace knew exactly where he was.
2 Samuel 9:1 says David asked, “Is there still anyone left… that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
Not because of Mephibosheth.
Because of covenant.
Read that again.
He wasn’t sought because he was worthy—he was summoned because he was remembered.
And that changes everything.
Because Ephesians 2:4–5 says that while we were dead in our trespasses, God—being rich in mercy—made us alive with Christ.
Dead.
Not struggling.
Not improving.
Dead.
And still… pursued.
AHA REVELATION:
God’s grace is not a response to your condition—it’s rooted in His covenant.

You didn’t earn it.
You can’t maintain it.
You can only receive it.
But here’s the tension—
When they came to fetch Mephibosheth, he didn’t run toward the palace.
He feared it.
Because when you’ve lived in shame long enough, love feels suspicious.
He bows before David and says in 2 Samuel 9:8, “What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?”
That’s not humility.
That’s identity distortion.
That’s what happens when your past speaks louder than God’s promise.
SPIRITUAL MIRROR:
Some of you don’t reject God—you just don’t believe His kindness applies to you.

You worship… but at a distance.
You pray… but without expectation.
You serve… but still feel disqualified.
Because deep down, you’ve labeled yourself:

“Too broken.”
“Too late.”
“Too far gone.”
But David doesn’t correct Mephibosheth with a lecture.
He restores him with a seat.
He says, “You shall eat at my table always.” (2 Samuel 9:7)
Always.

Not until you improve.
Not until you heal.
Not until you prove yourself.
Always.
And that…
That is the Gospel.
Because Jesus is the greater King.
Where David restored a seat, Jesus restores a soul.
Romans 5:8 says while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

Not after we cleaned up.
Not after we fixed our mess.
While we were still in it.
This is where religion gets uncomfortable.
Because religion says, “Fix yourself, then come.”
Jesus says, “Come, and I will fix what you cannot.”
Conviction line:
Some people are more committed to looking holy than being healed.
And it’s keeping them in Lo-debar.
Because this is where it gets personal.
What if the very thing you’re hiding is the place grace is trying to reach?
What if your limp is not your limitation… but the stage where God will reveal His mercy?
Paul said in 2 Corinthians 12:9, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is made perfect in weakness.”
Not despite it.
In it.
IDENTITY SHIFT:

You are not the sum of what broke you.
You are the evidence of what Christ can restore.
You are not disqualified—you are invited.
And here’s the beauty no one talks about—
When Mephibosheth sat at the king’s table, his crippled feet were hidden under it.
Covered.
Not removed.
Covered.
Just like Colossians 3:3 says your life is now hidden with Christ in God.
The King didn’t erase his story.
He redefined his position.
Grace doesn’t always remove the scar—
But it will always rewrite the ending.
So here’s the invitation.
Come out of hiding.
Come out of Lo-debar.
Come out of the quiet compromises, the delayed obedience, the silent exhaustion.
Repent—not just of sin, but of believing you are beyond grace.
Turn back to Jesus.
Not halfway.
Not later.
Now.
Because the same King who called Mephibosheth is calling you.
By name.
And there is a seat with your name on it.
Stay hungry for truth.
If this pierced something in you…
And listen—
The next message might be the one that pulls you all the way out of Lo-debar.
